Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered for their potential in crowd connectivity scenarios, wherein a large number of devices attempt to connect to a single MIMO base station. In these scenarios, researchers have proposed unique access protocols such as XL-MIMO to ensure efficient data transfer. A key aspect of XL-MIMO protocol effectiveness lies in its theoretical foundation, specifically the concept of visibility areas. According to the proposed scheme, successful data transfer is only possible when the signal from the base station and the signal from the device reach the same point in the network. This condition is defined as the area where the visibility area of the device overlaps with that of the base station. In cases where the devices are positioned randomly, researchers have used probability theory to determine the likelihood of this event occurring. Recently, studies have explored the statistical characteristics of visibility areas in large-scale MIMO systems, revealing that in many instances, the visibility areas of multiple devices do not intersect with the base station's visibility area. In contrast, other research has found that under certain circumstances, the visibility areas of multiple devices may overlap with each other. The current study extends these findings by investigating the distribution of visibility area intersections for multiple devices in XL-MIMO systems. Furthermore, the study derives the probability of all devices' visibility areas intersecting with the base station's visibility area. The results demonstrate that the distribution of visibility area intersections for multiple devices can be described using a similar model as the visibility areas themselves. The study also finds that the probability of all devices' visibility areas intersecting with the base station's visibility area can be determined using the same approach used to determine the probability of all areas falling within the visibility of the base station. The research provides a foundation for further investigation into the characteristics of visibility area intersections in XL-MIMO systems, as well as its potential applications in queueing theory and performance analysis. The results are available online for the benefit of the scientific community. The author recommends that future research explore the statistical characteristics of visibility areas in various large-scale MIMO systems and the development of performance analysis models for such areas. Neural network-generated text has gained popularity recently; however, its flaws in capturing grammar and syntax rules have been well-documented. This leads to issues when using such generated text in tasks like language model fine-tuning and generation of conversational AI. A neural network-generated text system is proposed, which utilizes a neural network as a starting point and fine-tunes it using $n$-gram linguistic models to fill grammar and syntax gaps. This system is tested on English language generation and compared to existing methods like bigram and trigram replacement, demonstrating its superiority by achieving the best results on grammaticality evaluation and human assessment. This system's capabilities are further demonstrated through applications in creation of language models for low-resource languages and generation of technical articles on mathematics and computer science. The system's ability to learn complex structures like passive voice is also verified. The code and models are available for use by the community.

Initially, we aim to validate the claim that iOCR outperforms conventional OCR in vote tabulation, as suggested by a previous study. Secondly, we endeavor to compare the performance of different iOCR software alternatives - specifically, the current preferred method utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) followed by OCR-enhanced text recognition, as opposed to using the software to recognize shapes and then translating them into characters. Lastly, we appraise the practical applicability of iOCR in accurately counting votes, given its requirement for pre-defined ballot templates, which may pose difficulties in its implementation for various ballot types. Throughout the investigation, we utilize a diverse range of ballot templates from multiple sources, demonstrating the iOCR method's effectiveness in capturing vote tabulations, while also identifying potential limitations and challenges associated with its use. Consequently, we contend that iOCR represents the most precise technique available for this purpose, followed by the shape recognition method, and then the conventional OCR approach. Furthermore, we observe that the iOCR method excels in accuracy compared to the conventional OCR method, although the differences are relatively minor. Finally, we advocate for the implementation of the iOCR technique in election ballot count tabulation, while also recommending future research on developing automated ballot template creation technologies.

The paired-permutation test has gained popularity recently, particularly in evaluating the performance of learning from rankings due to its effectiveness in addressing structured test data. However, the test operates with a significance level, and meeting it does not guarantee the desired level of precision for practical applications. In contrast, a test with a given precision threshold for learning from rankings is more desirable. Therefore, we introduce the precise paired-permutation test that aims at achieving specific precision levels. The new test is equivalent to the paired-permutation test in terms of statistical properties but requires the same level of theoretical support. We also provide an analytical formula for calculating the exact test statistic under the alternative hypothesis, which serves as a key component in proving the test's asymptotic superiority. As a result, we can seamlessly integrate the precise paired-permutation test into typical statistical inference scenarios. Furthermore, we illustrate its superiority over the standard test on real-world data sets. The precise paired-permutation test is available for use, having been developed into a manageable R function. Its asymptotic properties mirror those of the standard test, enabling us to conclude equality in large samples and concluding the test's efficacy for normally distributed data. The precise paired-permutation test outperforms the standard test in all tested situations, demonstrating its effectiveness in structured test metrics.
